text: Measuring whether hardening actually worked — because importing a baseline, enabling ASR rules, and turning on Credential Guard are not, by themselves, proof any of it is actually in effect on a given machine.

A baseline GPO is linked to an OU as planned, but weeks later a different admin links a more specific GPO to a child OU for an unrelated reason, and it happens to set one overlapping setting. Because of normal GPO precedence, the newer, more specific GPO quietly wins on that setting for every machine underneath it. Nobody changed the baseline, nobody got an error — the setting simply never applied where it was supposed to, and the only way to know is to check the machine itself. Running gpresult /h report.html /f produces an RSoP report showing exactly which GPO won each setting.

GPO precedence is only one way a setting can silently fail to apply. A WMI filter can quietly exclude a machine from the baseline. Slow-link detection can skip some settings entirely over a poor connection. And a setting can simply be unsupported on that particular machine's OS build. None of these show up as an error — they just mean the baseline isn't actually protecting that machine.

Real measurement runs in layers. A tool like Policy Analyzer confirms a setting actually landed by diffing the baseline against live local policy. Microsoft Secure Score tracks hardening posture as a trend over time, genuinely useful for reporting progress to leadership. But neither proves a control stops a real attack — that takes a tabletop exercise walking through a scenario conceptually, or a red team actually attempting the technique against real, hardened systems.

A red team runs a Mimikatz credential-dumping attempt against 20 hardened workstations. On 18, Credential Guard blocks it exactly as designed. On 2, it succeeds — those machines were imaged before the baseline existed and never received the GPO, a gap the Secure Score had been climbing past for months without ever seeing it.

A compliance scan confirms the setting is there; a red team or tabletop confirms it actually stops something; only the combination catches a gap like that for real.
